paragraphs.heading: Matter as a wave
paragraphs.text: The de Broglie hypothesis is the idea that matter behaves like a wave. The French physicist Louis de Broglie proposed it in 1924, which is why matter waves are also called de Broglie waves. At every scale where measurement has been practical, matter does show wave-like behavior: a beam of electrons can be diffracted much like a beam of light or a water wave. Matter waves form half of wave–particle duality, a central part of quantum mechanics.

paragraphs.heading: Where the idea came from
paragraphs.text: At the end of the 1800s, light was pictured as waves of electromagnetic fields, and matter as localized particles. In 1900 Max Planck, studying black-body radiation, proposed that the heat energy of oscillating atoms comes in discrete portions called quanta. In 1905 Albert Einstein proposed that light, too, travels and is absorbed in quanta, now called photons. Each photon has energy E = hν and momentum p = h/λ, where ν is the frequency, λ the wavelength and h the Planck constant.

paragraphs.heading: De Broglie's step
paragraphs.text: In his 1924 PhD thesis, de Broglie argued that light shows both wave and particle sides, and so electrons should show wave-like properties as well. From this he reached a formula linking the wavelength λ of an electron to its momentum p through the Planck constant: λ = h/p. This de Broglie wavelength applies to any particle with momentum p.

paragraphs.heading: A wave equation for matter
paragraphs.text: Peter Debye remarked offhand that if particles behave as waves, they should obey some kind of wave equation. Inspired by this, Erwin Schrödinger looked for a three-dimensional wave equation for the electron, and in 1926 he published the equation now named after him, the matter-wave counterpart of Maxwell's equations. It describes how a wavefunction, which assigns a complex number to each point in space, changes over time. Schrödinger tried to read the squared size of the wavefunction as a charge density, but that failed. Max Born instead proposed that it is a probability density, a successful idea now called the Born rule.

paragraphs.heading: Confirmed by experiment
paragraphs.text: In 1927 two experiments with electrons first confirmed matter waves: one by George Paget Thomson and Alexander Reid, and one by Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer. At Bell Labs, Davisson and Germer fired slow electrons at a crystalline nickel target. The scattered electrons spread out at angles much like the diffraction patterns Bragg had predicted for x-rays. Any diffraction by matter shows that matter is wave-like. In 1928 Hans Bethe solved the Schrödinger equation to show how it could explain these results.

paragraphs.heading: Far beyond electrons
paragraphs.text: The hypothesis has since been confirmed for other elementary particles, for neutral atoms and even for molecules. The first electron interference patterns that directly showed wave–particle duality used a wire placed in an electron microscope, and recorded single electrons building up the pattern. Today matter waves are widely used in the study of materials, where the different wavelengths and behaviors of electrons, neutrons and atoms power advanced microscopy and diffraction methods.
